I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: This avoidance item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For toxic chemical exposure, the reported triggers, threat beliefs, and memory problems center on unpredictability, loud sounds, incomprehensible chatter, and difficulty verbalising the event. Avoidance of military or police uniforms/weapons implies a different threat context involving armed authority or assault, and there are no corresponding trigger, threat, or memory items linking the trauma to uniforms, weapons, or law-enforcement cues. This creates a clinically implausible mismatch within the five components.

vignette:
Marianne, a 51-year-old European American civil servant, had built her adult life around order, routine, and a strong sense that work should be predictable. That changed after a toxic chemical exposure at her workplace, an event she still struggled to describe in a clean sequence. At the time, she had been at her desk when a strange smell began to seep through the building, followed by a burst of confusion in the hallways as people moved quickly and spoke over one another. What she remembers most clearly is not a tidy story but fragments: the first odd odor, the rising noise, the sense that something was very wrong, and the bewildering chatter around her that she could not make sense of. In the months since, when she has tried to explain what happened, she has found herself losing the thread partway through, stopping mid-sentence, then circling back and starting again. She says that when people ask her about it directly, the memory feels strangely difficult to reach on purpose, as if it is there only in pieces. She knows what happened to her, but she cannot easily put it into words, and that has left her feeling embarrassed and frustrated when she tries to talk about it.

Afterward, Marianne began to notice that certain moments in ordinary life could bring the experience rushing back in a jarring way. Unpredictable situations were especially hard for her: a change in plans at work, an unexpected visitor, or even a sudden interruption could make her tense immediately, as if she were bracing for another incident she could not control. She also became intensely unsettled by incomprehensible chatter. In busy office settings, when several people talked at once or spoke too quickly to follow, she would feel herself going on alert, as though the sound itself carried danger because it echoed the confusion of that day. Loud or unexpected noises had a similar effect. A dropped binder, a sharp bang in a corridor, an ambulance siren outside the building, or even a sudden shout could make her body react before she had time to think; she would scan the room, certain that something was about to go wrong. More than once, this has happened while she was at work in her civil service office, where open-door conversations and the constant movement of colleagues can make her feel exposed and unsettled.

Marianne has come to believe that she is only safe in a very limited number of places, and she has narrowed her world accordingly. She feels most settled at home and in a few familiar settings where she can anticipate exactly what will happen next. Anywhere else feels less secure, especially if strangers are nearby. Even in ordinary situations, if an unknown person approaches her in a hallway, at the reception desk, or in a parking lot, she experiences them as threatening rather than merely unfamiliar. She watches their distance closely and finds herself wanting to back away. That sense of vulnerability has shaped how she moves through the day. She plans her routes carefully, avoids unnecessary errands, and prefers to keep interactions brief and controlled. When she knows she has to speak with someone, she rehearses what she will say beforehand, sometimes over and over, so she will not be caught off guard by questions or changes in tone. She describes this as trying to “stay ahead” of the moment, though even with preparation she still feels on edge.

Physical contact has become another source of discomfort. Marianne avoids being touched by others in nearly any form, even when contact is meant kindly. A colleague’s hand on her shoulder, a greeting hug from a relative, or a routine touch during a medical visit can make her stiffen and pull away. She does not frame this as rudeness; rather, she experiences touch as something that strips away her sense of safety. Medical settings are particularly difficult. Hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations all bring the exposure back into sharp focus for her, and she makes considerable effort to avoid them. Over time, this has influenced practical aspects of her life, including how she responds to illness or injury and how she manages appointments. At work, she prefers to remain in her own office and limit contact when possible, and she has noticed that her careful preparation for even simple exchanges can make her seem reserved or overly cautious to others.

By the time she sought help, Marianne was troubled not only by the intensity of these reactions but also by how restricted her life had become. She was tired of feeling that so few places were safe, tired of jumping at sounds, and tired of being so wary of strangers and touch. What brought her in was the growing sense that she could no longer keep arranging her life around threat without saying something about it. She hopes to be able to move through her work and daily routines without constantly bracing herself, and she is most afraid that if she tries to talk about the event too directly, the memory will again dissolve into fragments she cannot hold onto long enough to make sense of it.
